summary:
Nebraska's state-level framework for trans visitors is set by Executive Order No. 23-16, signed by Governor Jim Pillen on 30 August 2023. The order establishes a Women's Bill of Rights and defines sex, female, male, woman, girl, man, boy, mother and father for use by state agencies, stating that biological sex is determined at birth and that biological differences between males and females in athletic ability and safety warrant sex-based segregation in some athletic, social and educational spaces. The order backs single-sex spaces for women's sports, bathrooms and changing rooms. Pillen was the second U.S. governor to sign such an order. Opponents questioned the order's scope and legality.

State documents are correspondingly restrictive. A legal gender marker change on a Nebraska birth certificate requires a notarized affidavit from the physician who performed sex reassignment surgery together with a certified copy of a court order changing the applicant's name. A driver's licence or state ID change requires a court order certifying the change and/or a physician-signed form confirming sex reassignment surgery. A name change requires district court paperwork, a court date, and publication for four consecutive weeks, or two weeks for minors. These requirements apply to state-issued documents; a visitor holding an out-of-state or foreign passport is not directly governed by them, but a trans person resident in Nebraska or seeking Nebraska-issued identification faces them.

Participation rules for trans students in Nebraska athletics have tightened in stages. The Nebraska School Activities Association requires transgender students to show evidence of hormone replacement therapy and/or sex reassignment surgery. In June 2025 Legislative Bill 89, banning transgender athletes from any sports, passed the unicameral legislature by a two-thirds majority and was signed by Governor Pillen; ten transgender athletes were identified as affected.

Gender-affirming healthcare for people under 19 is barred in Nebraska. The legislature passed the ban 33-15 in May 2023 and Governor Pillen signed it effective immediately. The Nebraska Supreme Court upheld it 6-1 in July 2024. A trans visitor under 19 cannot obtain this care in the state, and a visitor of any age cannot obtain it for a minor in their care.

Custody is a documented site of harm specific to Nebraska. A transgender woman diagnosed with gender dysphoria and transitioning while held in Nebraska's men's prison sued prison officials and workers; on 10 August 2022 U.S. District Judge Brian C. Buescher ruled for the defendants, dismissing her claims of failure to treat her dysphoria, denial of gender-conforming surgery, and failure to protect her. Nebraska had housed her by assigned sex at birth among male prisoners and placed her in a cell with a convicted male sex offender who sexually assaulted her. The judge had earlier dismissed the failure-to-protect claim over that placement, wrote that without medical evidence no reasonable jury could conclude the providers were deliberately indifferent to her serious medical need, and said she had not plausibly alleged more than de minimis injuries from the assault. He found no support for inferring a substantial risk from a prospective cellmate's sexual-offence conviction coupled with the alleged vulnerability of a transgender inmate transitioning to a woman in a men's prison. The placement followed her within the system.

Protection machinery is uneven. Nebraska's 1997 hate crime law guarantees the right to live free from violence or intimidation by threat of violence and enhances sentences for manslaughter, assault, terroristic threats, stalking, kidnapping and false imprisonment, rape and sexual assault, arson, criminal mischief and trespassing. It does not address gender identity. Federal law has covered gender identity under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act since 2009. The state Supreme Court upheld the hate crime law in April 2016, in a case protecting even a straight victim in the company of gay friends.

Discrimination protection for trans people in Nebraska rests on federal rulings and municipal ordinances rather than statewide statute. Employment discrimination on the basis of gender identity became illegal under Bostock v. Clayton County, decided 15 June 2020. In August 2020 the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission announced it would investigate and resolve housing discrimination claims on account of sexual orientation or gender identity, applying the same ruling to housing. Federal enforcement followed: from 11 February 2021 the Fair Housing Act prohibition on discrimination because of sex was enforced to include sexual orientation and gender identity, with HUD accepting, investigating and enforcing complaints of anti-trans housing discrimination covering sale, rental, terms, conditions and services. Omaha has prohibited discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment and public accommodations in both the public and private sectors since 2012, when the City Council voted 4-3 on 13 March to amend the city's anti-discrimination laws to add sexual orientation and gender identity as protected classes, with an exemption for religious institutions. Lincoln passed a 5-0 ordinance in February 2022 covering employment, accommodation and housing, but the protections were removed in June 2022 after a petition drive. In November 2021 the Nebraska State College System voted 4-2 to include gender identity in its policy.

Conversion therapy aimed at changing gender identity is outlawed in Lincoln under a 2021 ordinance and remains lawful in the rest of Nebraska. Statewide ban bills were reintroduced in 2021 and 2025 but have not passed.

Marriage and family recognition are settled in Nebraska as a matter of federal law. Same-sex marriage has been legal since Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015, with then Attorney General Doug Peterson directing compliance and non-enforcement of contrary Nebraska laws. That replaced a constitutional ban adopted in November 2000 by 70 per cent to 30 per cent defining marriage as the union of a man and a woman. A trans visitor in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship can marry and have that marriage recognised. Nebraska permits adoption by same-sex couples and single LGBT individuals: the Lancaster County District Court ruled for the plaintiffs in Stewart v. Heineman on 5 August 2015, the Nebraska Supreme Court upheld that ruling in April 2017 striking down the ban on same-sex foster parents, and in March 2021 it held that state adoption law clearly allows a same-sex married couple to adopt.

Sodomy prohibitions in Nebraska were repealed by a revised criminal code enacted in June 1977, effective 1 July 1978, by a veto override of 32-15 against Governor J. James Exon.
tangentialFactors:
The practical weight of Nebraska's state measures depends on how long a visitor stays and what they need from state institutions. A short-stay visitor using only federal documents and private accommodation encounters the state framework mainly through facilities practice and the absence of a statewide gender-identity discrimination statute. A trans person resident in Nebraska, or a visitor needing Nebraska-issued identification or care, meets the marker requirements, the under-19 care ban and the athletics rules directly.

A trans visitor in a relationship that Nebraska authorities would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has full marriage and adoption recognition, so the usual concern about partner recognition in hostile jurisdictions does not arise here. The exposure lies elsewhere: in facilities, in custody if arrested and held in state or county detention, and in the absence of a statewide hate-crime or anti-discrimination provision naming gender identity.

Enforcement of the 1997 hate crime law is documented in a case the state Supreme Court decided in April 2016 protecting a straight victim in the company of gay friends, which indicates the statute is applied to perceived-association bias, but nothing in the state's own law extends that to gender identity. Federal protection under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act covers gender identity, so a bias-motivated offence against a trans person can be charged federally even where state law is silent.

outOfScopeNotes:
The Hill report on the governor signing Executive Order No. 23-16 could not be retrieved; the publisher returns a 403 error to automated fetches. Its content is corroborated by the governor's own press release, the Jurist report and local coverage, so the underlying facts are not in doubt, but the article text itself was not read.

The inventory does not record Nebraska measures on bathroom access beyond Executive Order No. 23-16's endorsement of single-sex spaces, does not record whether any Nebraska city or the state has adopted a facility-use enforcement provision, and does not record state-level statistics on violence against trans people in Nebraska. No figure for trans homicide or assault victimisation in Nebraska is sourced here, so none is stated.

Several provisions in the national layer are in litigation or have been enjoined, and the operative position on those federal measures should be checked before travel. That layer is carried by the national record.

The inventory does not record Nebraska's current rules on gender markers for state-issued documents after the 2023 executive order, so whether any state agency has narrowed marker practice beyond the statutory surgery requirements described here is unresolved on the sources reviewed.
